A proposal for agentic development

Claude writes the code. little-workshop keeps it governed.

little-workshop is a self-hosted system that runs the whole lifecycle of a software project, from requirement to deployed server, and gives Claude Code a defined, checked route through every step. Agents get real branches, real tests and real gates. People get one place to hand out work, watch it happen and decide what ships.

12pillars, each its own process
138MCP tools for Claude
26policies, each a test script
3,661unit tests, all passing
9projects managed today

01 · Why it exists

An agent that can write code is not yet a teammate

Claude Code can implement a feature, fix a bug or rewrite documentation in minutes. What it cannot do on its own is follow a team's way of working: which branch to start from, which tests prove the change, which rules a commit must satisfy, who approves the merge, how the server is redeployed and what happens when something breaks at night.

Without that structure, agentic development stalls at one of two places. Either every agent step needs a person standing next to it, which removes most of the gain, or the agent is trusted with raw git, deploy and publish commands, which nobody should accept for production work.

little-workshop is the structure. It absorbed five separate tools (requirements tracking, gitflow versioning, an issue-to-agent runner, a package index and a project bootstrapper) into one system where every action, by a person or by Claude, goes through the same routes and the same checks.

For developers

Hand a task to Claude, review the result

Describe the work. Claude gets its own branch, runs the tests, writes a seven-section change report and opens a pull request. You decide whether it is finished.

For the team

Rules that hold every time

Branch naming, version bumps, requirement citations, test coverage and tag formats are code, checked at commit, at branch finish and before release or deploy, for people and agents alike.

For whoever pays

Usage you can see

Every Claude session is measured: tokens, cache efficiency, context size, cost at list price. The system finds wasteful patterns and proposes automations that run without the model.

02 · What it is

One daemon, three ways in

little-workshop runs on a developer machine as a set of small services. People and agents reach the same functions through three thin front ends that hold no data of their own.

For people

The Dashboard

A web app (also installable on a phone) with every project, task, job, policy, requirement and schedule. Pages update live as work progresses. Reachable on the machine and, through Tailscale, from anywhere you are signed in.

For Claude

The MCP server

138 tools named workshop_<area>_<action>: start a branch, record a test run, finish a branch, deploy, read the queue. Claude Code sessions use them instead of raw commands, and each project's settings decide which run freely and which ask first.

For terminals and scripts

The lws command line

The same operations as commands, for example lws version feature-start, lws requirements run-tests or lws job list. Useful in scripts, hooks and CI.

The key property: because the Dashboard, the MCP tools and lws are all thin proxies over the same services, a rule enforced once applies to everyone. A branch finish that a policy blocks is blocked whether a person clicks a button, a script calls lws or Claude calls a tool.

03 · How work flows

Every action is a Job, and every Job can be gated

Creating a requirement, starting a branch, running tests, building, publishing a package, deploying a server and running a Claude task are all Jobs. A Job is created by whoever asks (a person, Claude, a schedule or a trigger), passes through the policy gate, and is then dispatched to the service that owns that kind of work. Its steps, timings and result are recorded and shown live.

  1. Something asks. A person in the Dashboard, Claude through a tool, a script through lws, a schedule at 02:00 or a trigger such as "a branch finished".

  2. Orchestration records a Job with its type, project and parameters, and puts it on the project's queue so two conflicting actions never run at once on the same project.

  3. The policy gate checks it. Every policy attached to that kind of action (for example branch_finish or deploy_redeploy) runs as a sandboxed test. If one fails, the Job waits in pending_confirmation and shows up on the Dashboard as needing attention.

  4. The owning service does the work and reports each step as it goes: what it is doing, how long it took and how long it usually takes.

  5. Everyone sees the same result. The Job page, the task list, the calendar, statistics and the requester all read the same record.

04 · How it is built

Small independent services, supervised, with nothing shared but interfaces

little-workshop is written in Python (FastAPI) and built with Bazel. Each area of responsibility is a pillar: its own process, its own SQLite database, its own configuration folder and one versioned HTTP interface on a local Unix socket. No pillar reads another pillar's database or imports its code. That boundary is what makes the rest possible:

A crash stays local

Each pillar is a systemd --user service. If one crashes, Core (a small supervisor that holds no data) relaunches its last good build at once. The other pillars keep working, and so does any task in progress elsewhere.

Upgrades without downtime

A pillar is redeployed alone: the new commit is checked out in a scratch worktree, checked that it imports cleanly, installed, and only then is the old process stopped. little-workshop upgrades itself this way, one pillar at a time, in dependency order.

Off means off

Optional pillars, such as Image Generation or the always-on MCP pillar, start no process at all until the manifest enables them.

Interfaces, not internals

Pillars find each other through Core and talk over /v1/… routes. A new interface version can run beside the old one, so callers upgrade on their own schedule.

WhereWhat lives there
~/.config/little-workshop/manifest.tomlCore's list of pillars, which are enabled and how to start them.
~/.config/little-workshop/<pillar>/Each pillar's own settings, written by that pillar only.
~/.config/little-workshop/projects/<project>/Per-project files; the file name says which pillar may write it (manifest.deployment.toml).
~/.local/state/little-workshop/Each pillar's SQLite database, the sockets, worktrees and installed pillar code.
Each project's repositoryIts code, its docs/, its VERSION, the generated .claude/ files and git hooks. Git stays the source of truth for versions.

05 · The pillars

Twelve responsibilities, each with an owner

Orchestration jobs

Every Job, its queue and its steps. Schedules (once or on weekdays), triggers ("when X happens, run Y"), queue capacity per project, the policy gate and the live change feed the Dashboard follows.

Policy & Compliance rules

Policies written as a plain-language rule plus a pytest script, run in a sandbox. Decides which projects each policy governs and at which gate points it blocks; holds failing actions for a person.

Registry & Portfolio projects

The list of projects, creating new ones (scaffold, git, dev branch, optional GitHub repo) or importing existing ones, each project's backlog, and the generated Claude configuration of every project.

Requirements & Quality proof

Requirements in EARS form, test suites, results (pytest or any JUnit-XML), test runs in a sandboxed checkout, and the Definition-of-Done report: done means published, linked to tests, and those tests passed.

Version Control & Release git

Gitflow as a service: feature, improvement, hotfix, release and support branches, release candidates, version hooks that write VERSION, branch audits and a "stabilize" sweep. Merges only through its own finish commands.

Build & Packages artifacts

Runs a project's build in an isolated worktree, records the run, and hosts packages: a PyPI-compatible index and a VS Code extension store, refusing to publish anything built from a fork.

Deployment & Servers running things

Starts, stops and redeploys project servers: build before stop, a health probe, optional Tailscale exposure and a confirmation window with automatic rollback. Also redeploys little-workshop's own pillars.

Agentic Development Claude

Runs Claude Code tasks on real branches, read-only queries, interactive sessions you can open from the Claude app, documentation updates from review comments, incident reports, and Blender asset exports.

Dashboard people

The web interface described in chapter 11. Holds only its own preferences and day-by-day statistics; everything else it reads live from the other pillars.

MCP Server tools

Translates each of 138 tools into one interface call. Started by each Claude Code session (lws mcp serve), so it always matches the installed version.

Usage & Efficiency cost

Collects what every Claude session uses (telemetry, hooks, transcripts), flags wasteful patterns, proposes automations that need no model, and tells unattended jobs to wait when the plan's usage is high.

Image Generation optional

A queue for pictures rendered on a local ComfyUI: batching, automatic restarts, detection and re-rendering of bad (grey) outputs, verified downloads, and a GPU usage report agents read before GPU work.

06 · Agentic development

What happens when you give Claude a task

A task is the unit of agentic work: a title, a description and a project. Everything else (branch, tests, report, review) is handled by the system, the same way every time.

  1. You describe the work on the New task page, from a backlog entry, or through workshop_agent_run_task. You choose the kind of work (task, bug, docs, milestone), the review mode, whether Claude may read the shared engineering standards, and whether it may generate images.

  2. The branch is prepared first. little-workshop starts the right gitflow branch, or checks out the one you named, before Claude starts. When the branch is specified, Claude is forbidden to touch branches at all; the prompt says so and the project's guard hook refuses raw git checkout, merge or push.

  3. Claude works in the project with the project's own instructions, permissions and MCP tools, a browser it can drive (Playwright) to check web UIs, and Remote Control, so you can watch or answer it from the Claude app. The task page also shows a live "peek" at what it is doing.

  4. It must say how it went. The run ends with AGENT_STATUS: done, partial or failed. A missing or unreadable status counts as partial, never done.

  5. It writes a change report in seven fixed sections: background, goal, technical decisions, executed tasks, screenshot, test results and pull-request link. The report becomes the PR description, so review starts from the explanation.

  6. You decide. In manual review the task waits as awaiting finish until you finish or skip it. In auto-approve it finishes only if Claude reported done and its recorded test run passed. Either way, the finish goes through the same policy gate as any person's.

Hard rules, in code
  • Automation never merges, deletes, finishes or releases on its own initiative.
  • One agent task per project at a time; other projects run in parallel.
  • Tests run in a sandboxed checkout, never in the working copy.
  • A crashed or cut-off run fails visibly and opens an incident.
Other kinds of Claude work
  • Queries: read-only questions answered from a project's checkout.
  • Sessions: an interactive Claude session for a project, or one across all projects, opened from your phone.
  • Docs updates: highlight text in a document, comment, and Claude revises the docs on a branch.
  • Incidents: an unexpected error becomes a card; confirming it starts a fix task.

07 · Governance as code

Rules are scripts, checked at the moment they matter

A policy is a rule written in EARS form ("WHEN a commit is made, the commit's VERSION file shall have a higher version than its parent's") plus a pytest script that proves it against a project. New policies can be described in plain language: Claude drafts the EARS text and the script, checks them, and files a draft that does nothing until a person approves it.

Each policy chooses which projects it governs, whether it blocks in each (a non-gating check still runs and is recorded), and at which gate points it applies:

commitbranch_finishreleasepackage_publishbuild_installserver_launchserver_stopdeploy_redeployself_redeployproject_registrationproject_removal

At commit

The commit hook

Each project's .githooks/commit-msg runs the policies gating commit and refuses a commit that breaks one, printing the rule and the fix. A pre-commit hook writes VERSION on working branches.

Before a finish

The preflight skill

Claude runs policy-preflight before finishing a branch or releasing: the same checks the gate will run, in a sandbox, nothing recorded, so failures are fixed while the change is still open.

At the action

The gate

The real check. A failing policy holds the Job for a person. There is also a time-limited, logged bypass a person can switch on from their own terminal (sudo lws bypass_policies true --time 5); Claude cannot.

Requirements and the Definition of Done

Requirements live in the Requirements pillar and in docs/requirements.md. Tests carry markers such as # --- REQ-000000442: … ---; a sync links them to their suite. A recorded test run in a sandbox marks each linked requirement passed or failed, and a branch finish can require it.

Versions

Every commit raises VERSION (0.2.73-dev.7 on a branch), release candidates are tagged v0.2.73-rc.1, and production tags must sit on production history. All of it is checked by policy, not by memory.

08 · Claude, configured

Every project gets the same instructions, permissions and guard

little-workshop generates each project's Claude Code configuration from one template and keeps it in sync. A project's own additions are preserved; the generated parts cannot be edited by hand, so every project follows the current rules.

Generated fileWhat it does
.claude/settings.jsonThe permission table. Every MCP tool and lws command is classified exactly once: read-only and routine ones run freely, policy-gated ones run because the gate protects them, and human decisions (confirming a held action, resuming a paused queue, deleting files, generating images) always ask.
.claude/hooks/lws_scope_guard.pyA hook that refuses, with the right route to take instead: calls naming another project, raw git merge/tag/push, systemctl, twine or gh pr merge, hand edits of generated files, and, in unattended runs, decisions only a person may take.
.claude/little-workshop.mdThe shared briefing every project's AGENTS.md imports: who runs the lifecycle, what is enforced, and how to ask for images.
Skillsworkshop-lifecycle (the routes for branches, releases, deploys, test runs), policy-preflight and policies-digest.
Scope by design. A Claude session opened inside a project can only act on that project. Work across projects happens from a session in the workspace root, which is the only place with wider permissions.
Usage & Efficiency

Every session's tokens are collected from telemetry, hooks and transcripts. The Claude usage page shows weighted tokens per day, cache hit ratio, average context per request and long-context share. Detectors turn patterns into findings, repeated tool sequences become plugin proposals in the backlog, and unattended jobs wait while the plan's five-hour usage is high.

Shared standards

A task can include a read-only copy of the shared engineering standards (testing, requirements, agent tasks, project conventions), compiled from the policies and kept current by a catalog job.

09 · Automation

Schedules, triggers and a catalog of safe jobs

Job catalog

The jobs a person can start from the Dashboard are a fixed list with typed options, never free text: build project, run tests, release, export Blender assets, update standards documentation, optimize Claude usage, apply common Claude configuration, configure telemetry.

Schedules

Any job or task can run once at a set time or every chosen weekday at a time. Examples running today: the weekly release of little-workshop, nightly usage ingestion and analysis. A run missed while the machine was off becomes a question, not a surprise.

Triggers

"When an event happens, run a job": when a branch of little-workshop finishes, redeploy the pillars it changed; when a Claude session ends, ingest its transcript. Triggered jobs are gated like any other, and no trigger may merge, finish, release, remove or delete.

Queues

Jobs on the same project share a queue, one at a time by default. A queue's capacity can be raised, inspected and released.

10 · How to use it

From install to a finished, Claude-built feature

Set up once
  1. Install with bazel run //:install: it installs lws and registers the MCP server with Claude Code. Core then starts every pillar the manifest enables as a user service.
  2. Open the Dashboard at http://localhost:8790 (add it to your phone's home screen through Tailscale).
  3. Add projects: New project creates one; workshop_project_import registers an existing repository and writes its Claude files and git hooks.
  4. Attach the policies each project should follow on the Policies page.
Every day
  1. Jot ideas in the project's Backlog; let Claude refine one into a task prompt.
  2. Launch the task (or start a branch yourself with lws version feature-start and work with Claude interactively).
  3. Follow it on the task page, or answer it from the Claude app.
  4. Review the change report and PR, then Finish: the policies run and the branch merges into dev.
  5. Release on a schedule or by hand; redeploy servers from the Dashboard.

12 · Bringing it to a team

What carries over, and what a company setup needs

little-workshop was built for one machine and up to two developers, and it has been used daily on nine projects (Python services, a SvelteKit app, C++, two Unity games) since mid-September 2026: 377 commits, with the system building, testing, versioning and redeploying itself the whole time. The ideas are the valuable part, and they do not depend on that scale.

Carries over as is
  • Agent tasks on real branches with a fixed report and a human finish.
  • Policies as code, checked at commit, preflight and gate, for people and agents alike.
  • Generated, uniform Claude configuration with a guard hook per project.
  • Requirements linked to tests and a sandboxed Definition of Done.
  • Usage measurement per session, project and origin.
Needs work for a company
  • Users and roles: today the trust model is "the people on this machine". A team needs sign-in, roles and an audit of who approved what.
  • Hosting: pillars run as user services on Linux (WSL here). A shared server or one install per developer needs deciding.
  • Integration: GitHub is supported; GitLab, Jira or the company CI would need adapters.
  • Secrets and network: the Dashboard is reached over loopback or Tailscale; company SSO and secret storage would replace that.
  • Claude access: sessions run on Claude Code with the developer's plan; a company would choose team plans or API keys.

A pilot that answers the question quickly

  1. Two weeks, one team, one service. Install on the developers' machines and import one real repository.

  2. Encode three rules the team already follows as policies (for example version bump, requirement citation, test coverage) and gate branch finishes on them.

  3. Route ten real tickets through agent tasks with manual review, and measure review time, rework, test results and Claude cost per merged change on the Claude usage page.

  4. Decide from those numbers which parts to adopt, and whether to invest in the multi-user work above.
